newsitem.title: USA: Elvis empire all shook up by Houston bar.
newsitem.headline: Elvis empire all shook up by Houston bar.

text.p: A Houston bar has got Elvis Presley Enterprises Inc. all shook up.
The business empire left behind by the late Presley has sued a tavern called the Velvet Elvis in hopes of forcing it to change its name.
It said the bar besmirches the image of the King of rock-and-roll and infringes on the corporation's trademarks.

Bar owner Barry Capece testified on Tuesday in federal court that the Velvet Elvis was named after a velvet painting of the singer, not Elvis himself. The painting hangs on a wall in the bar not far from a velvet painting of a topless Mona Lisa.
Capece told U.S. District Judge Vanessa Gilmore the Velvet Elvis was intended to be a "cheesy, tacky, off-the-wall parody" of a Las Vegas lounge.

But Carol Butler, director of worldwide licensing for Memphis, Tennessee-based Elvis Presley Enterprises, testified on Monday that the bar was an affront to the dignified image of the singer that his estate tried to uphold.
"It's not the kind of place I would go," she said.

Capece told the court that the Elvis motif in his bar was minimal, but Presley attorney Mack Webner pointed out that the menu included a peanut butter-and-banana sandwich, which he described as the singer's "favorite food."
Presley died in 1977 at his Graceland estate in Memphis.

Webner said in opening arguments that Capece named his bar the Velvet Elvis because "Elvis sells." Butler testified that Elvis Presley Enterprises plans to open an Elvis Presley restaurant in Memphis in the near future.
Capece opened the Velvet Elvis in 1991. He said financial problems forced him to close the bar in 1993, but he reopened it in another location a year later.

In March Capece opened a sister bar -- The Velvet E -- in Dallas and said he plans to start another one soon in Denver. He said he shortened the name of the Dallas bar to avoid further legal problems.
Testimony in the case was expected to wrap up as early as Tuesday afternoon but Gilmore was not likely to rule for several weeks, defence attorney Terry Fitzgerald said.
